newsitem.title: UK: NatWest jumbo loan securitisation seen as success.
newsitem.headline: NatWest jumbo loan securitisation seen as success.

text.p: NatWest's innovative jumbo loan securitisation for nearly $5.0 billion has been well-received by investors, syndicate managers said on Thursday.
"The deal is an attractive piece of paper for the markets, and congratulations should go out to NatWest," said a securitisation expert at a rival British bank.
"They had a good idea, and roadshows were well-managed to build interest," he said.
NatWest formally launched its 11-tranche FRN today, just over a month after plans for the deal were made public. Officials there were unavailable for comment.
The deal's innovative structure turned about $5.0 billion worth of high-quality, low-margin corporate syndicated loans into securities, freeing up around 200 million stg of NatWest's capital.
Most of the deal's tranches, issued by special purpose vehicle ROSE Funding, were rated double-A, lower than the triple-A rating carried by most securitised paper.
"Investors were happier to buy a double-A bond with a bit more yield than they would have been to buy triple-A rated paper at a tighter spread," said a syndicate manager at a U.S. bank.

The British banker added: "There has been demand for higher-yielding securitised paper for some time, but for most borrowers it is more expensive to issue paper with a lower rating because of the yield differential."
"In this case, double-A was the best rating the transaction could carry because NatWest's own credit rating was the ceiling," he said.
Dealers said other banks might consider following NatWest's example in order to be able to re-invest capital in businesses with higher returns than the syndicated loans market.

"A lot of bank liability committees will now look at their own conditions. We will not see extensive copycating, but I would be disappointed if some banks did not follow," said a syndicate manager at a European bank.
He said British banks were more likely to follow suit because regulation in most other European countries made securitisation difficult.
